Compliance of Selected Electronics Manufacturing Companies with E-Waste Management Rules in India

An Analytical Study of Five Leading Firms

Name: Laxmi Bonde (24102A0049)

Satyam Revgade (24102A0035)

ABSTRACT

Electronic waste is a growing environmental and public-health concern in India, particularly because significant quantities can move through informal collection and recycling channels. This study reviews the publicly stated e-waste practices of five Indian electronics manufacturers: Dixon Technologies (India) Limited, Kaynes Technology India Limited, Sahasra Electronics Private Limited, Centum Electronics Limited and Syrma SGS Technology Limited. The comparison focuses on E-Waste Rules compliance, Extended Producer Responsibility (EPR), use of authorised recyclers, source segregation, hazardous-substance controls and related environmental practices. The study is based on public disclosures and does not constitute an independent facility audit. It also identifies disclosure gaps and recommends stronger quantitative reporting, formal-sector integration and clearer public information.

Keywords: E-waste, EPR, RoHS, authorised recycling, corporate compliance, source segregation, India.

INTRODUCTION

Rapid growth in electrical and electronic equipment has improved connectivity, productivity and quality of life, but it has also increased discarded equipment and demand for raw materials. Electronic products may contain hazardous substances, making collection, storage, dismantling and recycling important environmental-management functions.

The supplied analytical study notes that India generated about 3.2 million tonnes of e-waste in 2019 according to the Global E-waste Monitor 2020, while CPCB estimated 10,14,961.2 tonnes for 21 types of EEE in 2019-20 based on sales data from 1,380 producers. Despite a formal legal framework, informal handling remains a major challenge.

This report therefore compares five formal-sector electronics manufacturers to understand the practices they publicly state they follow for e-waste collection, segregation, channelisation, recycling, EPR and hazardous-waste management.

MATERIAL AND METHOD

The study is analytical and comparative. It relies on the E-Waste (Management) Rules and amendments, the Hazardous and Other Wastes (Management and Transboundary Movement) Rules, CPCB guidance on EPR, corporate sustainability and website disclosures, environmental-management certifications, and secondary literature. The evidence is documentary: no independent physical inspection or compliance audit of company facilities is claimed.

OVERVIEW OF THE APPLICABLE LEGAL FRAMEWORK IN INDIA

• E-Waste (Management) Rules: establish producer responsibility and require environmentally sound channelisation of e-waste through authorised systems.

• Extended Producer Responsibility (EPR): places end-of-life responsibility on producers where applicable and links collection/recycling obligations to the producer role.

• Hazardous and Other Wastes Rules, 2016: regulate storage, transport, import/export and disposal of hazardous waste categories.

• RoHS requirements: restrict specified hazardous substances such as lead, mercury, cadmium, hexavalent chromium, PBB and PBDE in applicable electrical and electronic equipment.

• Environmental and occupational requirements: include pollution-control, safe handling and workplace obligations relevant to manufacturing and waste management.

COMPANY-WISE ANALYSIS OF E-WASTE RULES COMPLIANCE

1. Dixon Technologies (India) Limited

Dixon is a major electronics manufacturing services company with a predominantly B2B contract-manufacturing model. Its public practices include channelising e-waste to government-authorised recyclers, applying EPR requirements where relevant, following Reduce-Reuse-Recycle principles and maintaining source segregation.

The supplied study also identifies Dixon's RoHS controls for lead, mercury, cadmium, hexavalent chromium, PBB and PBDE, and reports a Zero Waste to Landfill approach. Direct consumer take-back is described as generally not applicable to its B2B model, with consumer-facing responsibility resting mainly with brand owners. No specific e-waste violation was identified in the reviewed disclosures.

2. Kaynes Technology India Limited

Kaynes provides design-led electronics system design and manufacturing services. Its disclosed e-waste practices include collection, storage and disposal through CPCB-authorised recyclers and registered agencies, application of EPR requirements relevant to its operations, and use of authorised agencies for recycling, refurbishment and final disposal.

The company also reports 3R practices, source segregation and controlled handling. The exact scope of consumer take-back depends on whether Kaynes acts as a producer for a particular product category. The reviewed material did not identify a specific current e-waste rule as publicly not followed.

3. Sahasra Electronics Private Limited

Sahasra manufactures electronic components and assemblies and is presented in the source study as having formal EPR Authorisation and E-Waste Management Authorisation. It reports collection facilities, PAN-India collection capability, reverse logistics and channelisation to a recycler/dismantler registered with the Haryana State Pollution Control Board.

Sahasra also maintains authorised collection/drop points and an ISO 14001:2015 Environmental Management System. The source study therefore describes Sahasra as one of the more formally documented entities in the five-company sample. No specific e-waste regulation was publicly identified as not followed.

4. Centum Electronics Limited

Centum serves specialised aerospace, defence, industrial and medical electronics markets. Its disclosed practices include collection, segregation and storage of e-waste before disposal, use of approved authorised e-waste recyclers, recycling/reuse, and a Reduce-Recover-Reuse approach.

The company also reports authorised waste vendors and controlled hazardous-waste storage, transport and final disposal. Because much of its customer base is institutional or defence-related, consumer-oriented take-back has limited practical applicability, while facility-level environmental obligations remain applicable.

5. Syrma SGS Technology Limited

Syrma SGS is a design and manufacturing services company with documented internal controls and customer-facing instructions. Its stated practices include EPR requirements, authorised dismantling/recycling, proper collection, transport, storage and segregation, authorised collection points and maintenance of e-waste tracking and disposal records.

The company instructs customers to use authorised collection or recycling points and not to dispose of e-waste through informal scrap channels, municipal garbage or landfill waste. No specific e-waste regulation was publicly identified as not followed in the reviewed material.

COMPARATIVE SUMMARY OF COMPLIANCE PRACTICES

Note: “None” means no specific violation was identified in the reviewed public disclosures; it is not an independent audit finding that every legal requirement has been fulfilled.

FINDINGS, DISCUSSION AND RECOMMENDATIONS

Across the five-company sample, the source study reports a consistent formal-sector pattern: all five use authorised dismantling or recycling channels, maintain source segregation and state that they follow environmentally sound disposal practices. Dixon, Kaynes and Syrma SGS explicitly reference EPR; Sahasra holds formal EPR and e-waste authorisations; and Centum emphasises statutory environmental requirements and authorised disposal.

Distinctive practices include Dixon's Zero Waste to Landfill commitment and detailed RoHS substance controls, and Sahasra's ISO 14001:2015 certification and PAN-India collection infrastructure. A major limitation is the lack of granular public data on actual e-waste quantities collected, formally recycled and achieved against collection/recycling targets.

1. Mandatory quantitative disclosure: publish annual e-waste generated, collected and channelised to authorised recyclers, with progress against EPR targets.

2. Strengthen B2B accountability: contract manufacturers and brand owners should coordinate and verify functional take-back and EPR systems.

3. Integrate the informal sector through training, registration and links with authorised facilities while improving labour and environmental standards.

4. Expand separate collection infrastructure and consumer incentives, including deposit-refund approaches where appropriate.

5. Support technology and research for hazardous-waste monitoring and cleaner recovery of valuable materials.

6. Improve public information on State Pollution Control Board portals, especially lists of authorised collectors and recyclers.

CONCLUSION

The five companies examined - Dixon Technologies, Kaynes Technology, Sahasra Electronics, Centum Electronics and Syrma SGS Technology - illustrate that formal electronics manufacturers can institutionalise important elements of e-waste management, including source segregation, authorised recycling, EPR-related practices and environmentally sound disposal. Selected companies also report Zero Waste to Landfill, RoHS controls or ISO 14001 certification.

At the same time, corporate practices alone cannot resolve India's broader e-waste challenge. The source study highlights limited quantitative disclosure, continued informal-sector activity and the separation between contract manufacturing and brand-owner take-back responsibilities. Stronger monitoring, public reporting, formal integration and awareness are therefore important complements to company-level compliance.
